cover.question: Why did her smile shock?
cover.name: ÉLISABETH VIGÉE LE BRUN
cover.answered_by: She showed her teeth: in art an open mouth meant the poor, the mad or children; a critic called it an affectation condemned by all people of taste, worse in a mother

facts.claim: Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Madame Vigée Le Brun and Her Daughter Julie, 1786, oil on wood, 105 × 84 cm, Musée du Louvre (INV 3069)
Her open smile showing her teeth shocked critics: the self-portrait with her daughter was shown at the Paris Salon of 1787
She smiles with her teeth visible; per Colin Jones (The Smile Revolution in Eighteenth-Century Paris, 2014) this was unusual in elite portraiture
Jones: an open mouth in Western art had very negative connotations: plebeian, insane or demented, or children who had not attained the age of reason
Jones: eighteenth-century teeth were often bad, linked to sugar consumption

A commentator (Jones: anonymous; Artnet: the Mémoires secrets) condemned 'An affectation which artists, art-lovers and persons of taste have been united in condemning … in smiling she shows her teeth. This affectation is particularly out of place in a mother.'
Comparison image: Frans Hals, Malle Babbe (c. 1640), Gemäldegalerie Berlin, an open-mouthed laughing figure

caption:
This smile shocked Paris.

In 1786 Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Marie Antoinette's portrait painter, painted herself hugging her daughter Julie, and she showed it at the Paris Salon of 1787. Look closely: her lips are parted, and you can see her teeth.

That was the problem. As the historian Colin Jones explains, in Western art an open mouth had long belonged to the poor, the mad or small children, the people who couldn't control themselves, like Frans Hals's laughing Malle Babbe. And in an age of sugar, real teeth were often bad. Elegant sitters kept their lips closed.

One commentator was outraged. Smiling so that she shows her teeth, he wrote, was "an affectation which artists, art-lovers and persons of taste have been united in condemning", and "particularly out of place in a mother".

🖤 Would you have smiled for your portrait?
